content: The history of biochemistry extends over approximately 400 years. Although the term biochemistry was first used in 1882, it is widely accepted that the word was formally proposed in 1903 by Carl Neuberg, a German chemist. Initially, it was believed that the processes of life were not governed by the same scientific laws as non-living matter. It was thought that only living organisms could produce the molecules essential for life, derived from pre-existing biomolecules. However, in 1828, Friedrich Wöhler published a groundbreaking paper demonstrating the artificial synthesis of urea, proving that organic compounds could be created outside of living organisms. By the late 1700s and early 1800s, it was known that stomach secretions could digest meat and that plant extracts and saliva could convert starch into sugars. However, the mechanisms behind these processes were not understood. In the 19th century, Louis Pasteur studied the fermentation of sugar into alcohol by yeast and concluded that this process was catalyzed by a vital force within the yeast cells, which he called ferments. He asserted that alcoholic fermentation was linked to the life and organization of yeast cells, not their death or decay. In 1878, Wilhelm Kühne, a German physiologist, introduced the term enzyme, derived from the Greek word enzymon, meaning in leaven, to describe this process. Over time, the term enzyme came to refer to non-living substances like pepsin, while ferment was used to describe chemical activity produced by living organisms. In 1897, Eduard Buchner began studying yeast extracts and their ability to ferment sugar in the absence of living yeast cells. Through experiments at the University of Berlin, he discovered that sugar fermentation occurred even without living yeast cells. He named the enzyme responsible for sucrose fermentation zymase. In 1907, Buchner was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his discovery of cell-free fermentation. Following Buchner's work, enzymes were typically named based on the reactions they catalyzed, such as DNA polymerase, which synthesizes DNA polymers. The realization that enzymes could function outside living cells led to efforts to determine their biochemical nature. Early researchers observed that enzymatic activity was associated with proteins, but some scientists, including Nobel laureate Richard Willstätter, argued that proteins were merely carriers for the true enzymes and were not themselves capable of catalysis. This debate was resolved in 1926 when James B. Sumner demonstrated that the enzyme urease was a pure protein and successfully crystallized it. He later crystallized the enzyme catalase in 1937. The definitive proof that pure proteins could act as enzymes came from the work of Northrop and Stanley, who studied digestive enzymes such as pepsin, trypsin, and chymotrypsin. These scientists were awarded the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The ability to crystallize enzymes eventually enabled their structures to be determined using X-ray crystallography. This was first achieved for lysozyme, an enzyme found in tears, saliva, and egg whites that digests bacterial cell walls. The structure of lysozyme was solved by a team led by David Chilton Phillips and published in 1965. This high-resolution structure marked the beginning of structural biology and the effort to understand enzyme function at the atomic level. The term metabolism originates from the Greek word metabolismos, meaning change or overthrow. The scientific study of metabolism has a history spanning 400 years. The first controlled experiments on human metabolism were conducted by Santorio Santorio, who published his findings in 1614 in his book Ars de statica medicina. He described weighing himself before and after various activities such as eating, sleeping, working, fasting, and excreting. He discovered that most of the food he consumed was lost through what he termed insensible perspiration. Since then, biochemistry has advanced significantly, particularly in the mid-20th century, with the development of techniques such as chromatography, X-ray diffraction, NMR spectroscopy, radioisotopic labeling, electron microscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations. These methods facilitated the discovery and detailed analysis of cellular molecules and metabolic pathways, including glycolysis and the Krebs cycle (citric acid cycle). One of the most influential biochemists of this era was Hans Krebs, who made substantial contributions to the study of metabolism. He discovered the urea cycle and, in collaboration with Hans Kornberg, elucidated the citric acid cycle and the glyoxylate cycle. Today, the findings of biochemistry are applied across diverse fields, including genetics, molecular biology, agriculture, and medicine.
